title: 24 — Design S3-like Object Storage
html:
24 — Design S3-like Object Storage

The one idea: separate metadata (bucket, object name → object ID, version) from data (immutable bytes). The data store is simple — append many small objects into large files, locate them by (file, offset, size) — and durability comes from replication or erasure coding across failure domains.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Buckets; upload/download objects; versioning; list objects in a bucket (by prefix).
  • Objects from KB to GB; 100 PB in one year; six nines durability (99.9999%), four nines availability.
  • Storage efficiency: reduce cost while keeping durability.

Storage types, briefly

Block File Object
Mutable Yes Yes No (replace whole object)
Access Raw blocks (SAN, disks) Hierarchy, POSIX HTTP API, flat namespace
Scale Medium High Vast
Use VMs, DBs General file sharing Backups, media, data lakes, static sites

Object storage properties: objects are immutable, key-value (URI → bytes), write once read many, small and large objects alike.

Step 2 — High-level design

---
title: Object storage — high-level architecture
---
flowchart LR
    C["Client"] --> LB["Load balancer"] --> API["API service<br/>(stateless)"]
    API --> IAM["IAM<br/>(authn/authz)"]
    API --> MS["Metadata service"] --> MDB[("Metadata store<br/>bucket, object → uuid")]
    API --> DS["Data store"]
    subgraph DS["Data store"]
        PS["Placement service<br/>(cluster map, heartbeats)"]
        DN1["Data node (primary)"] --> DN2["Data node (replica)"]
        DN1 --> DN3["Data node (replica)"]
    end

Upload flow

  1. Authn/authz via IAM.
  2. API sends bytes to the data store → returns object UUID.
  3. API writes metadata (bucket_id, object_name, object_id, version).

Download flow

  1. Metadata lookup: (bucket, name) → UUID.
  2. Data store: UUID → bytes.

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Data store

  • Placement service keeps the cluster map (DC → rack → node → disk) via heartbeats; picks nodes for new data across failure domains. Runs as a small Paxos/Raft cluster.
  • Data nodes replicate: primary receives write, replicates to secondaries, acks when enough succeed (consistency vs latency dial again).

3.2 How data is organised on a node

Storing each object as a separate file wastes inodes and disk blocks for small objects. Instead:

  • Append small objects into a large read-write file; when it reaches a size (e.g. GBs) seal it as read-only.
  • An object mapping table (per node, e.g. SQLite/RocksDB) stores object_id → (file_name, start_offset, size).
  • Writes are serialised per file (or one active file per CPU core).

3.3 Durability

  • Hardware failure: a disk's annual failure rate ~0.8%; 3 replicas → ~six nines.
  • Failure domains: replicas in different racks / AZs / regions.
  • Erasure coding (e.g. 8 data + 4 parity chunks): survives any 4 lost chunks.
3× replication Erasure coding (8+4)
Storage overhead 200% 50%
Durability ~six nines ~eleven nines
Write/read cost Cheap CPU for encode/decode; reads touch multiple nodes
Use Hot data Warm/cold data, most of the volume
  • Correctness: checksums (e.g. MD5/CRC) per object and per file; verify on read; background scrubbing.

3.4 Metadata data model

bucket  (bucket_name, bucket_id, owner_id, enable_versioning)
object  (bucket_name, object_name, object_version, object_id)

Object table is huge → shard by hash(bucket_name, object_name) (spreads evenly, supports point lookups).

Listing by prefix is the awkward query across shards: scatter-gather to all shards with pagination cursors per shard, or a denormalised listing table sharded by bucket.

3.5 Versioning

Insert a new row with a new object_version (TIMEUUID) instead of overwriting. Delete inserts a delete marker as the newest version.

3.6 Large objects: multipart upload

  1. Initiate → upload ID.
  2. Upload parts in parallel (each with an ETag); retry individual parts.
  3. Complete with the part list → the service assembles the object; garbage-collect parts.

3.7 Garbage collection

Deleted, orphaned (failed uploads), and corrupted data is marked and later compacted: copy live objects into a new file, update the mapping table, delete the old file.

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Metadata/data separation, append-file layout, replication vs erasure coding, failure domains, checksums, versioning with delete markers, multipart upload, and GC/compaction.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Azure Blob Storage is this system: containers = buckets, block blobs with StageBlock/CommitBlockList = multipart upload, blob versioning and soft delete, immutability (WORM) policies, lifecycle management to cool/cold/archive tiers.
  • Redundancy options map to the durability discussion: LRS (3 copies in one DC), ZRS (across AZs), GRS/GZRS (plus a secondary region); Azure uses erasure coding internally.
  • Access: SAS tokens (prefer user-delegation SAS) or managed identity + RBAC; Azure.Storage.Blobs SDK with TransferOptions for parallel uploads.
  • Listing by prefix: GetBlobsByHierarchyAsync(prefix: "photos/2026/", delimiter: "/"); ADLS Gen2 adds a true hierarchical namespace for data-lake workloads.

Review checklist

  • Block vs file vs object storage.
  • Metadata vs data separation; upload/download flows.
  • Small objects packed into large files + mapping table.
  • Replication vs erasure coding with numbers; failure domains.
  • Versioning, multipart upload, GC.
  • Prefix listing across shards.
